oral treatment with antibiotics disrupts the normal ecology of the intestinal tract, allowing overgrowth of enteric bacteria, which in turn promotes translocation of these organisms to the mesenterics lymph nodes.

antibiotic treatment of mice disrupts the normal intestinal ecology, allowing an enteric bacilli overgrowth in the intestine, which in turn leads to an increased translocation rate of these enteric bacilli into the mesenteric and systemic sites.

oral treatment of specific pathogen-free mice with antibiotics disrupts the normal microbial ecology, allowing an enteric bacilli overgrowth in the gastrointestinal tracts and promoting their translocations to the mesenteral lymph nodes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the normal flora in preventing the translocation of gram-negative enteric organisms from the gastrointestinal tract to the mesenteries, liver, and spleen of animals.
the effects of antibiotics and the normal flora on translocation from the gut to the lymph nodes.
the translocation of gram-negative enteric bacterial pathogens from the gastrointestinal tractors of mice to the mesentery lymph nodes, spleen, liver, kidneys, lungs, and blood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

oral treatment of mice for 4 days with penicillin or clindamycin promotes the translocation of gram-negative enteric pathogens from the gastrointestinal tract of mice, and this effect is more pronounced after clindamyciin treatment than after penicillin therapy.

the oral treatment of mice for only 4 d with antibiotics that are used in human medicine to treat infections of the gastrointestinal tract (penicillin, clinda mycin, and metronodazole) can promote the translocation of the gram-negative enteric bacilli from the gastrointestinal tract.

the oral treatment of mice for 4 days with clindamycin or penicillin promotes the translocation of gram-negative enteric organisms from the gastrointestinal tract of mice, and this translocation is not promoted by the oral treatment of the mice with metronidazole.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oral treatment of mice, rats, or rabbits with antibiotics disrupts the normal intestinal flora ecology and increases the translocation of bacteria to the mesenteral lymph nodes.

the disruption of the normal intestinal microflora ecology by antibiotics can promote the translocation of gram-negative enteric organisms from the gastrointestinal tract of mice to the mesenterical lymph nodes, and that the disruption of this normal microflora ecology can be produced by the use of antibiotics which are not known to be associated with the development of the translocation phenomenon in patients.
antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal microbial flora and promotes translocation of enterobacteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the normal flora plays a major role in preventing the translocation of gram-negative enteric organisms from the intestinal tract to the mesentery lymph nodes.

the oral administration of penicillin, metronidazole, or clindamycin for a short time (4 days in this study) can cause a dramatic shift in the intestinal flora, allowing for the overgrowth and translocation of enterobacteriaceae.

the oral administration of antibiotics to mice, even in low doses for a relatively short period of time, can promote the translocation of gram-negative bacilli from the gastrointestinal tract to the mesentery lymph nodes.
